notes.b: The B-complex is a family of separate water-soluble vitamins that often occur together in the same foods. They are named by number or by name, and between them they keep energy release, nerves, skin and blood working.
points: The family includes B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin) and B6 (pyridoxine), plus folate and B12, which also belong to the B complex.

The B-complex vitamins act mainly as coenzymes (helpers that enzymes need in order to work), helping the enzymes that release energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein. They also keep the nervous system, skin and red blood cells healthy.
The B vitamins do not supply energy themselves. The energy comes from the carbohydrate, fat and protein in food, and the vitamins only help release it.

The B-complex vitamins are water-soluble, so any excess is excreted in urine. Most are not stored in the body in useful amounts, so they must be supplied daily in the diet. B12 is the exception, as it is stored in the liver.
Because they dissolve in water, B vitamins are also lost into cooking water and during storage.
Wholegrain cereals, meat, pulses and fortified breakfast cereals are the main dietary sources. Fish, eggs, milk and dairy, nuts, yeast extract and green vegetables also contribute.
White flour and polished rice lose much of their B vitamins in milling (grinding and refining the grain), whereas wholegrain products keep them.

The RDA (recommended daily allowance) is the amount that meets the needs of almost everyone. B vitamin needs rise with energy intake, especially thiamine and niacin, which are closely linked to energy release.
notes.tip: Vitamin B is a group, not one vitamin. If a question says just 'vitamin B', the answer expected is the release of energy from carbohydrate and fat. If it names niacin or thiamine, give that individual vitamin's job. Never say that B vitamins give you energy, and never say that none of them is stored.

notes.h: Vitamin B1 (thiamine): sources, functions and deficiency
notes.b: Thiamine is the B vitamin most closely tied to carbohydrate, so the more carbohydrate a person eats, the more thiamine they need. Without it the nerves, muscles and heart suffer.
points: Thiamine sources include wholegrain cereals and wholemeal bread, fortified breakfast cereals, pork and bacon, liver, pulses (peas, beans, lentils), nuts, yeast extract, eggs and potatoes.
Thiamine acts as a coenzyme that helps release energy from carbohydrate, so the need for it rises with carbohydrate intake.
Thiamine is needed for normal nerve function and keeps the muscles, including the heart, healthy. It also supports appetite.
Beriberi (beri-beri) is the thiamine deficiency disease, with loss of appetite, fatigue, weakness, muscle wasting, depression, irritability and memory loss.
Dry beriberi damages the nerves, causing tingling, numbness, pain, weakness and paralysis. Wet beriberi affects the heart, causing heart failure and swelling (oedema).
Heavy drinkers are at risk of deficiency because heavy alcohol use reduces the absorption of thiamine and the diet is often poor. This can lead to confusion and memory problems.
notes.tip: Beri-beri is the vitamin B1 deficiency disease asked in matching questions. Write it with a hyphen, as the Irish marking schemes do, and do not mix it up with pellagra (niacin) or cracked mouth corners (riboflavin). For a thiamine part, give two functions, one deficiency effect and one or two sources.

notes.h: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin): sources, functions and deficiency
notes.b: Riboflavin helps release energy from all three energy nutrients and protects the surfaces of the body, such as the skin, mouth and eyes. Its deficiency shows up mostly in these places.
points: Riboflavin sources include milk and dairy products (the largest contribution in many diets), eggs, liver and kidney, lean meat, yeast extract, green leafy vegetables, mushrooms and fortified breakfast cereals.
Riboflavin helps release energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein.
Riboflavin helps maintain healthy skin, eyes and mucous membranes (the moist linings of the mouth and other body passages), and it helps growth.
A deficiency causes sore, cracked lips and cracks and soreness at the corners of the mouth, known as angular cheilitis (also called cheilosis or angular stomatitis).
A deficiency also causes a sore, red, smooth, inflamed tongue and skin disorders, such as greasy, scaly skin around the nose.
Deficiency also causes sore eyes that are sensitive to light, and slow growth in children.
notes.tip: Cracked corners of the mouth point to riboflavin (B2), not niacin or thiamine. Remember it as the B vitamin of the skin, mouth and eyes.

notes.h: Niacin (vitamin B3): sources, functions and deficiency
notes.b: Niacin, also called nicotinic acid, is unusual because the body can make some of its own. It helps release energy and keeps three body systems healthy.
points: Niacin sources include meat (especially liver and poultry), fish, peanuts and other nuts, wholegrain cereals, pulses, mushrooms, eggs, milk, fortified cereals and yeast extract.
The body can make niacin from the amino acid tryptophan, found in protein foods such as milk and eggs. This is why milk and eggs prevent deficiency even though they contain little niacin.
Niacin helps release energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein in the cells.
Niacin keeps the skin, nervous system and digestive system healthy.
Deficiency causes pellagra, remembered as the four Ds: dermatitis (a skin rash in areas exposed to sunlight), diarrhoea, dementia (confusion and memory loss) and, if untreated, death.
Deficiency may also bring tiredness, weight loss and irritability. Pellagra was historically found where maize was the main food.
notes.tip: Pellagra and the four Ds belong to niacin. Do not say pellagra is caused by lack of vitamin C or vitamin D. Examiners accept tiredness, weight loss and irritability as extra deficiency effects.

notes.h: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): sources, functions and deficiency
notes.b: Pyridoxine is the B vitamin of protein use. It lets the body handle amino acids, build haemoglobin and make the chemicals nerves use to communicate.
points: Pyridoxine sources include chicken, turkey, pork, fish such as tuna and salmon, liver, eggs, potatoes, bananas, pulses, wholegrain cereals, nuts and fortified breakfast cereals.
Pyridoxine is needed for the breakdown and use (metabolism) of amino acids, so it is central to protein metabolism and growth.
Pyridoxine helps the body form haemoglobin in red blood cells, which is why deficiency can cause anaemia.
Pyridoxine takes part in making neurotransmitters, the chemicals that carry messages between nerve cells, so it supports the nervous system.
Deficiency is rare. It causes skin rashes around the mouth and nose, a sore mouth, confusion, depression, irritability, anaemia, and tingling in the hands and feet.
notes.tip: Link pyridoxine to protein metabolism, haemoglobin and neurotransmitters, and give anaemia as the deficiency effect.

notes.b: Exams often give a list of conditions and ask which vitamin is lacking in each. These pairs are worth learning as one set.
points: Night blindness is vitamin A, rickets is vitamin D and scurvy is vitamin C.
Beri-beri is vitamin B1 (thiamine) and pellagra is niacin (B3).
Neural tube defects are linked to folic acid. Megaloblastic anaemia is B12 (or folate) deficiency, and pernicious anaemia is B12 deficiency caused by a lack of intrinsic factor.
notes.tip: Matching questions have asked night blindness A, rickets D and beri-beri B1, and niacin with pellagra. Learn each condition with its vitamin as a pair.

notes.h: The other B-group vitamins: properties (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Being water-soluble, most B vitamins are lost into cooking water, and most are also sensitive to heat, light, alkalis or oxidation. Each vitamin has its own main weakness, and niacin and riboflavin are the more stable ones.
points: Thiamine is destroyed by alkalis (such as bicarbonate of soda) and by prolonged heat, and it is lost into cooking water. It is also destroyed by sulphur dioxide (sulphites) used as a preservative, but it is stable in acid conditions.

Riboflavin is destroyed by light (ultraviolet) and by alkalis, which is why milk in clear bottles loses riboflavin and is better stored in cartons or opaque bottles. Some is also lost in cooking water.
Riboflavin is heat-stable and acid-stable in normal cooking, and it gives a yellow-green colour to solutions that contain it, such as the yellow of some foods and urine.
Niacin is the most stable of the B vitamins. It is stable to heat, light, air, acid and alkali, so little is lost in normal cooking.
Niacin is soluble in water and can be lost into cooking water if the food is boiled and drained.

Pyridoxine is sensitive to light and alkali, and it is lost into cooking water. It is stable in acid conditions and fairly stable to heat in ordinary cooking, but is lost in the processing and milling of cereals.
notes.tip: For each vitamin, state that it is water-soluble and lost in cooking water, then name its destroyer: thiamine heat and alkali, riboflavin light, and niacin is stable.

keyTerms.definition: A non-protein helper molecule, often derived from a B-group vitamin, that allows an enzyme to carry out its reaction.
Vitamin B1, a water-soluble vitamin that helps release energy from carbohydrate and supports nerve function.
The deficiency disease caused by a lack of thiamine, with fatigue, weakness, nerve damage and heart problems.
Vitamin B2, a water-soluble vitamin that helps release energy and keeps the skin, eyes and mucous membranes healthy.
Cracking and soreness at the corners of the mouth, caused by a lack of riboflavin.
Vitamin B3, which the body can make from tryptophan and which helps release energy from food.
The deficiency disease caused by a lack of niacin, with dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia and death.
Vitamin B6, needed for the breakdown of amino acids and the formation of haemoglobin.
An essential amino acid from protein foods that the body can convert into niacin.
A chemical that carries nerve impulses across the gap between two nerve cells.

questions.prompt: Name two B-group vitamins and state the deficiency disease caused by a lack of each.
questions.model: Any two correctly matched pairs: thiamine (B1) causes beriberi; niacin (B3) causes pellagra; riboflavin (B2) causes cracks at the corners of the mouth and a sore tongue; pyridoxine (B6) causes skin rashes, confusion, depression and anaemia. One mark for each correct vitamin and one for each correct disease or effect.

questions.prompt: Discuss the role of the B-complex vitamins in releasing energy from food, giving the sources and the effects of deficiency for at least two named vitamins.
questions.model: B-complex vitamins are water-soluble and act mainly as coenzymes in energy metabolism; they are not stored in useful amounts so a daily dietary supply is needed. Thiamine (B1): wholegrain cereals, pork, pulses, nuts; releases energy from carbohydrate; deficiency causes beriberi with fatigue, weakness, memory loss and nerve or heart damage. Riboflavin (B2): milk, eggs, lean meat, liver, green vegetables, mushrooms; helps release energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein; deficiency causes angular cheilitis, a sore tongue and light-sensitive eyes. Niacin (B3): meat, poultry, fish, peanuts, wholegrain cereals, eggs; can be made from tryptophan; releases energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein; deficiency causes pellagra with dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia and death. Pyridoxine (B6): chicken, fish, pork, potatoes, bananas, pulses; needed for amino acid metabolism; deficiency causes skin rashes, confusion, depression and anaemia. Losses: thiamine and pyridoxine are lost into cooking water; riboflavin is destroyed by light.
